newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbians brave cold, police in New Year protest.
newsitem.headline: Serbians brave cold, police in New Year protest.

text.p: Thousands of opposition supporters braved bitter cold and a police ban to march through Belgrade banging pots, pans and drums in the latest mass protest against election fraud.
Some 10,000 students started the march through Belgrade on Wednesday evening and were soon joined by thousands more ordinary citizens.
The Zajedno (Together) opposition has planned another march for Thursday.
At least a quarter of a million people had earlier greeted the New Year in a city-centre rally which featured ringing alarm clocks as a shrill rebuff to President Slobodan Milosevic.
Wednesday's march was timed to drown out the evening news on state television, which is accused by the opposition of biased cover of the daily demonstrations of the past six weeks.
In its Wednesday evening broacast state television did not mention the huge rally held on New Year's Eve.

The Yugoslav news agency Tanjug said, almost 24 hours later: "some Belgraders assembled in Republic Square to usher in the new year to a programme in which Belgrade actors and alternative rock bands participated."
"The students are making a terrific din, banging pots and pans and people on sidewalks are also banging pots and pans."
The marchers were defying a ban by the Serbian ministry of the interior on their walks in the city centre.
But police allowed the march to proceed, keeping a low profile after the random beatings they handed out last week.
The autocratic Milosevic ended 1996 still ignoring the protests and telling federal Yugoslavia in his New Year's message it had been a very good year.

Western sources said Milosevic and Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic also snubbed a group of European Union diplomats who tried on Tuesday to deliver by hand a message urging democratic changes in Serbia.

The diplomats said they had the impression that Serbian authorities were ready to respond to pressure for democratisation, given teeth by Western threats to withhold financial aid for Yugoslavia's ruined economy.
A report by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) recommends that Milosevic acknowledge the Zajedno victories and initiate broader democratic reforms.
But diplomats in Belgrade believe the government is trying hard to postpone the decision as long as possible.
"We are now being told to expect a response some time next week," said one.
In the New Year message, broadcast on state television and radio, Milosevic pledged free market reforms in a possible sop to Western concerns.
He only obliquely alluded to the political crisis triggered by the annulment of election results that showed the opposition had won 15 of Serbia's 18 largest towns, including Belgrade.
